p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Children invent games long before anyone teaches them rules. A ball, a wall and a patch of open ground are enough; the rules are agreed, argued over and changed as the game goes on, and the point of playing is simply to go on playing. Organised sport takes this impulse and gives it structure: fixed rules, referees, leagues, coaches and, at the highest level, professional careers. The structure brings real benefits. It allows skill to be measured, rewards discipline and lets millions share the drama of a contest they could never play themselves.

Something can be lost in the process, however. When sport for the young is organised mainly as a pathway to selection, the child who is not chosen may conclude that sport is not for him at all, and give it up at the age when the habit of activity matters most. Practice becomes a duty to be completed rather than a pleasure to be sought, and the measure of success becomes the trophy rather than the game. None of this is an argument against coaching or competition. It is an argument for keeping, alongside the academy and the stadium, open spaces and unstructured hours in which anyone may play badly, cheerfully and for no reason beyond the enjoyment of it.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: The institutionalization of e-governance has been heralded as a democratizing panacea capable of eradicating bureaucratic inertia, minimizing administrative corruption, and streamlining public service delivery. By digitizing citizen-state interfaces, modern governments can bypass predatory intermediaries, ensuring that welfare disbursements, identity verifications, and regulatory approvals reach intended beneficiaries directly. However, this hyper-digital pivot exposes a deep systemic fault line: the digital divide, where marginalized populations lacking internet connectivity and digital literacy are effectively disenfranchised from state mechanisms. When essential civic resources become exclusively accessible through digital portals, the state inadvertently transforms technological privilege into a prerequisite for basic citizenship rights. Furthermore, centralized data architectural frameworks used for e-governance create massive surveillance apparatuses that significantly blur the boundaries between public welfare and invasive state monitoring. The true metric of successful e-governance is therefore not the sophistication of its algorithms or portals, but its structural inclusivity and its commitment to safeguarding civil liberties against digital overreach.

opts: Organised sport has real benefits, but space for free, unstructured play must also be kept.
Only professional sport deserves public support.
Coaching and competition harm young players.
Organised sport should be replaced by children's games.
questions.why: Main idea: the structure 'brings real benefits', yet the author argues 'for keeping... open spaces and unstructured hours'.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a benefit of organised sport?
opts: It lets millions share the drama of a contest.
It guarantees a professional career to every participant.
It allows skill to be measured.
It rewards discipline.
questions.why: Detail: the three benefits listed are measuring skill, rewarding discipline and sharing drama; careers come only 'at the highest level'.

questions.q: According to the passage, a child who is not selected may:
opts: Win more trophies in other sports.
Demand that the rules be changed.
Give up physical activity at an age when the habit matters most.
Become a better coach in later life.
questions.why: Inference/detail: the child 'may conclude that sport is not for him at all, and give it up at the age when the habit of activity matters most'.

questions.q: The author's attitude towards coaching and competition is best described as:
opts: Opposing them as harmful to children.
Praising them as the only purpose of sport.
Indifferent to their effects on the young.
Accepting them, while warning against making selection their chief aim.
questions.why: Tone: 'None of this is an argument against coaching or competition', but against sport 'organised mainly as a pathway to selection'.

questions.q: The word "impulse" in the passage most nearly means:
opts: Sudden injury
Cash reward
Natural urge
Written rule
questions.why: Vocabulary: organised sport takes the children's spontaneous urge to play and gives it structure.

questions.q: The phrase “democratizing panacea” shows that e-governance is initially seen as
opts: a system that will increase corruption
a cure-all for bureaucratic delays and poor service delivery
a tool only for tech-savvy groups
a corporate takeover of state assets
questions.why: A panacea is a remedy for everything. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: Complete digitisation of public services risks
opts: more predatory intermediaries
collapse of state data systems
disenfranchising people who lack digital access and literacy
ending the state's ability to monitor approvals
questions.why: Third sentence: the digital divide. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: When access to state services becomes exclusively digital, the author warns that
opts: technological privilege becomes a prerequisite for basic citizenship rights
welfare reaches every citizen instantly
the state loses its data authority
civil liberties are automatically protected
questions.why: Fourth sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: What dual nature of e-governance is highlighted?
opts: It cuts trade barriers but raises inflation
It streamlines welfare delivery but also enables invasive surveillance
It removes corruption but empowers intermediaries
It raises farm output but ignores cities
questions.why: Second and fifth sentences. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.

questions.q: According to the final sentence, good e-governance is measured by its
opts: algorithm speed and portal design
removal of civil liberties
partnerships with software firms
inclusiveness and protection against digital overreach
questions.why: Last sentence. Passage: GPSC pre-screening test (Junior Scale Officer), Jun 2026.
